grammar.name: 现在完成时
grammar.zh: have/has + 过去分词，表示过去发生、和现在有关的事，或从过去持续到现在
grammar.ex: Grandma has joined social media.

grammar.name: 现在完成时 + ever / never
grammar.zh: 问"有没有过"：Have you ever …? 回答常用 never
grammar.ex: I have never been so embarrassed in my life

grammar.name: already / yet
grammar.zh: already 用在肯定句"已经"；yet 用在否定句或疑问句句末"还（没）"
grammar.ex: She hasn't figured out the privacy settings yet.

grammar.name: for / since
grammar.zh: for + 一段时间；since + 过去某个时间点
grammar.ex: She has had her phone for only three weeks

grammar.name: 定语从句 who / which / that
grammar.zh: who 指人，which 指物，that 两者都可以
grammar.ex: the lady who lives next door

items.title: Grandma Has Joined Social Media
items.summary: 奶奶刚学会用社交软件，就开始给全家"惹麻烦"：在别人的照片下留言写长信、把孙子的尴尬旧照发到网上，最后却意外成了网红。
paras: My name is Kevin, and I am fourteen years old. I have had a phone for three years, and I have used social media for two. In that time, I have seen a lot of strange things online. I have seen cats that play the piano. I have seen people who eat forty hot dogs in ten minutes. But nothing has ever scared me as much as this sentence, which my mom said at dinner last month:
"Guess what? Grandma has joined social media."
I dropped my fork. My sister Jenny, who is sixteen, dropped her phone. My dad just closed his eyes and said, "Oh no."

My grandma is seventy-three. She is a wonderful person. She makes the best dumplings in the world. She knits sweaters for everybody, even for our dog. But Grandma and technology have never been friends. She has owned a microwave for twenty years, and she still doesn't know how to use the timer. She calls the TV remote "the clicker." She thinks the internet lives inside the computer, like a hamster.

Now, suddenly, Grandma had a smartphone. My uncle gave it to her for her birthday. She has had her phone for only three weeks, but she has already made an account on the most popular app. And she has sent friend requests to everyone. Everyone. Me, Jenny, my parents, all my cousins, her doctor, the lady who lives next door, and the man who fixed her washing machine in 2009.
At first, it was fine. Grandma posted a picture of her garden. Twelve people liked it. She was very happy. She called my mom and said, "Twelve people like my tomatoes! I have never been so popular!"
Then she discovered comments.
The first comment appeared under my photo. It was a picture of me and my friends at the basketball court. We were trying to look cool. Under it, Grandma wrote:
"KEVIN, IS THAT YOU? YOU LOOK TOO THIN. ARE YOU EATING ENOUGH? COME TO MY HOUSE ON SUNDAY. I WILL MAKE DUMPLINGS. ALSO, PLEASE CALL YOUR GRANDMOTHER MORE. LOVE, GRANDMA."
Everything was in capital letters. My friends saw it. Within one hour, they had all commented under it. "Kevin, call your grandmother!" "Kevin, are you eating enough?" "Can I come for dumplings too?"
I called Grandma. "Grandma," I said, "you don't need to write in capital letters. It looks like you are shouting."
"I am not shouting," said Grandma. "My eyes are old. Big letters are easier to read. Also, why didn't you call me? I have waited all week."
Jenny was next. She had posted a beautiful photo of the sunset at the beach. It was very artistic. She has worked hard on her photography for a year, and she was very proud of it. Grandma commented:
"Very nice. But where is your jacket? It is cold at the beach in the evening. You will catch a cold. Your mother never wore a jacket either, and she was always sick."

Then my mom saw it, and she commented, "Mom! That is not true!" And Grandma answered, "It is true. Do you remember 1994?" And then my aunt joined in, and my uncle, and soon there were forty-seven comments under Jenny's sunset photo. All of them were about my mom's health in 1994. Nobody said anything about the sunset.
"I have never been so embarrassed in my life," said Jenny. She hid her phone under her pillow for two days.
But the worst was still coming.

Grandma had found the button that lets you share photos. And Grandma has a very big box of old family photos. Hundreds of them. She has kept them since 1970. One Saturday morning, she decided to "share some memories."
The first photo she posted was my mom and dad's wedding. That was cute. The second photo was my uncle in the 1980s with very big hair. That was funny. The third photo was me.
I was three years old. I was in the bathtub. I was wearing nothing except a pirate hat and a lot of bubbles. I was holding a rubber duck and smiling like a crazy person.
Under the photo, Grandma wrote: "MY LITTLE KEVIN, THE BRAVE PIRATE. HE HATED BATH TIME, BUT HE LOVED THIS HAT. SO CUTE!!!"

I saw it at 9:15 in the morning. By 9:30, it had forty likes. By ten o'clock, it had two hundred. My whole school had seen it. My basketball team had seen it. And Sophie Martinez, the girl who sits next to me in science class, had seen it. She commented with three laughing faces and the words, "Arrr, matey!"
I ran to my parents' room. "Mom! Grandma has posted a picture of me in the bathtub! Everyone has seen it! My life is over!"
My mom tried not to laugh. She really tried. But her shoulders were shaking. "I'll call her," she said.
Grandma did not understand the problem. "But it is a beautiful picture," she said on the phone. "You were so cute. Why are you angry?"
"Grandma, you can't post private photos for everyone to see!" I said. "Have you checked your privacy settings?"
"What is privacy settings?"
That was the moment I knew. She hasn't figured out the privacy settings yet. Anyone in the world could see her page. Anyone in the world could see the brave pirate.

That afternoon, I went to Grandma's house. I sat with her at the kitchen table. I showed her how to change the settings. I showed her how to delete a post. I explained that some photos are for family only. I also explained the difference between a comment and a private message.
"So if I write a message, only you can see it?" she asked.
"Yes," I said.
"And if I write a comment, everybody can see it?"
"Yes."
She thought for a moment. "Then why does everyone write such strange things in public? Your cousin Mark wrote that he was 'dead' because of a funny video. I called his mother. I was very worried."
I laughed for five minutes.
We deleted the pirate photo. Grandma was a little sad, but she understood. Then something unexpected happened.

Before we deleted it, the picture had been shared more than three thousand times. People didn't really care about me. They cared about Grandma's comments. Someone had made a screenshot of her comment on my basketball photo, the one that said, "ARE YOU EATING ENOUGH?" And someone else had added the words, "Every grandma ever." It had gone viral. Thousands of people had shared it. They wrote things like, "This is exactly my grandma!" and "I need this woman to adopt me."

In one week, Grandma got more than two thousand followers. Strangers from all over the world asked her for her dumpling recipe. A woman from Australia asked her for advice about her son, who never calls her. A teenager from Canada asked her what to wear on a first date. Grandma answered every single one of them. In capital letters.
"I have never had so many friends," she told us at Sunday dinner. "Two thousand! Kevin, how many followers do you have?"
"Three hundred and twelve," I said quietly.
Grandma patted my hand. "Don't worry. You are young. Eat more dumplings, and one day you will be popular too."

Now Grandma has her own cooking videos. She makes dumplings and talks about life. Her most popular video has been watched eighty thousand times. In it, she looks directly into the camera and says, "Call your grandmother. She is waiting."

I call her every Wednesday now. Not because she asks me to. Well, partly because she asks me to. But mostly because I have learned something: my grandma is much cooler than me. And she has never once worn a pirate hat in public.

grammar.name: 过去进行时
grammar.zh: was/were + 动词-ing，表示过去某一时刻正在发生的事
grammar.ex: At six o'clock, Dad was driving Mom to the restaurant.

grammar.name: when / while 连接两个过去动作
grammar.zh: 长动作用过去进行时，打断它的短动作用一般过去时
grammar.ex: While we were decorating the living room, the dog was eating the cake.

grammar.name: 过去进行时与一般过去时对比
grammar.zh: 背景用进行时，发生的事件用一般过去时
grammar.ex: We were blowing up balloons when the doorbell rang.

grammar.name: 情态动词 should / might
grammar.zh: should 应该，might 可能（不太确定）
grammar.ex: They might be here in ten minutes!

grammar.name: 动名词作主语 / 宾语
grammar.zh: 动词-ing 当名词用：Keeping a secret is hard.
grammar.ex: Keeping a secret from my mom is like hiding the sun with a sock.

items.title: Operation Birthday Surprise
items.summary: 三兄妹给妈妈准备惊喜生日派对，计划很完美，执行起来一团糟：狗在吃蛋糕、爸爸在错误的时间回家，最后妈妈反而给了大家一个惊喜。
paras: Keeping a secret from my mom is like hiding the sun with a sock. She always knows. She knows when I haven't done my homework. She knows when I have eaten cookies before dinner. Once, she knew that I had broken a window, and she was at work at the time. So when my older brother Sam said, "Let's throw Mom a surprise party for her fortieth birthday," I thought it was a terrible idea.
"She'll find out," I said. "She always finds out."
"Not this time," said Sam. He is sixteen, and he thinks he is a genius. "This time, we have a plan."

The plan had a name. It was called Operation Birthday Surprise. Sam wrote it on a piece of paper and hid it inside a cereal box, because Mom never eats cereal. The plan was simple. Dad would take Mom out for dinner at six o'clock. While they were eating, Sam, our little sister Lily, and I would decorate the house. We would invite twenty guests. At eight o'clock, Dad would bring Mom home. We would turn off the lights and hide. When Mom opened the door, we would jump out and shout, "SURPRISE!"
"What could go wrong?" said Sam.
Everything. Everything could go wrong.
The first problem happened on the morning of the party. I was eating breakfast when Mom walked into the kitchen. She was holding the cereal box.
"I thought I might try some cereal today," she said. "Why is there a piece of paper inside?"
Sam was drinking orange juice at that moment. He made a noise like a broken vacuum cleaner. Orange juice came out of his nose.
I grabbed the box. "That's mine! It's... homework. Math homework. Very boring. You shouldn't read it."
Mom looked at me. Mom looked at Sam, who was still coughing. "Okay," she said slowly. "Math homework. In a cereal box." She smiled a strange smile and left the kitchen.
"She knows," I whispered.
"She doesn't know," said Sam. "Stay calm."
At six o'clock, Dad was driving Mom to the restaurant. We watched the car leave from the window. "Go, go, go!" shouted Sam. Operation Birthday Surprise had begun.

We worked fast. Lily, who is eight, was in charge of balloons. Sam was in charge of decorations. I was in charge of the cake. I had ordered a big chocolate cake from the bakery. It said "Happy 40th Birthday, Mom!" in pink frosting. It was beautiful. I put it on the kitchen table.

At half past six, the guests started to arrive. Our neighbors came. Mom's best friend, Carol, came. Mom's coworkers came. Grandma came with a big bag of presents. Everybody was whispering, because it was a surprise, even though Mom was not there.
We were blowing up balloons when the doorbell rang. It was Uncle Pete. Uncle Pete is very loud. He doesn't know how to whisper. "WHERE IS THE BIRTHDAY GIRL?" he shouted.
"She's not here yet!" we all whispered back.
"OH! RIGHT! THE SURPRISE!" he shouted. Then he tried to whisper, but his whisper was louder than most people's normal voice.
At seven o'clock, everything was almost ready. There were balloons on the ceiling. There was a big banner over the door. There was music ready to play. I went to the kitchen to check on the cake.
The cake was not on the table.

I looked under the table. And there was Biscuit, our golden retriever. He was lying on his back. His face was brown. His nose was pink. He looked like the happiest dog in the history of the world. Next to him, there was an empty cake box and a small piece of cake that said "Mom!"
"BISCUIT!" I screamed.
Sam ran in. Lily ran in. Uncle Pete ran in. Everyone ran in. While we were decorating the living room, the dog was eating the cake. All of it. Except the word "Mom."
Lily started to cry. Grandma started to laugh. Uncle Pete said, "WELL, AT LEAST HE LEFT THE IMPORTANT PART!"
"We need a new cake," said Sam. He was starting to panic. "The bakery closes at seven-thirty. Max, take your bike. Go! Now!"

I rode my bike faster than I have ever ridden in my life. I arrived at the bakery at 7:28. The lady was locking the door. I begged her. I told her about the dog. She felt sorry for me, and she sold me the last cake in the shop. It was a big white cake with blue flowers. On top, in blue frosting, it said, "Congratulations on Your Retirement, Bob!"
"It's all I have," said the lady.
I took it. There was no time to argue.

When I got home, Sam had another problem. He was holding his phone, and his face was white. "Dad just texted," he said. "Mom wants to come home early. She says she has a headache. They're leaving the restaurant now. They might be here in ten minutes!"
"Ten minutes?" said Carol. "Everybody, hide!"

What happened next was chaos. Twenty-two people tried to hide in one living room. Grandma hid behind the curtains, but her feet were showing. Two neighbors hid under the table. Uncle Pete tried to hide behind a lamp. He is six feet tall, and the lamp is very thin. Lily hid in a cupboard. I put Bob's retirement cake on the table and covered the word "Bob" with a banana. It was the best I could do.
Sam turned off the lights. "Nobody move," he whispered. "When the door opens, wait for my signal."
We waited in the dark. We were all breathing very quietly. Someone's stomach was making noises. Biscuit, who was still full of chocolate cake, was snoring.
Then we heard the car. We heard footsteps. We heard keys in the door.
The door opened. The light came on.
But it wasn't Mom. It was Dad. Alone. He was holding a pizza box.
"Why is it so dark in here?" he said.
Twenty-two people jumped out and shouted, "SURPRISE!"
Dad screamed. He threw the pizza into the air. The pizza landed on Uncle Pete. Grandma came out from behind the curtains and fell over the dog.
"Where's Mom?" shouted Sam.
"She's in the car!" said Dad. "She's on the phone with her sister! I came in first to check that everything was ready!"
"Well, it is NOT ready now!" said Sam.
Then we heard another voice from the door. A calm, amused voice.
"Is this a bad time?"

It was Mom. She was standing in the doorway. She was looking at the balloons, the pizza on Uncle Pete, Grandma on the floor, the sleeping chocolate dog, and the cake that said "Congratulations on Your Retirement, Ba" because the banana had slipped.
For a moment, nobody said anything.
Then Mom started to laugh. She laughed so hard that she had to sit down on the floor next to Grandma. Everyone started laughing. Even Sam.

"I knew," Mom said when she could finally speak. "I knew since this morning. The 'math homework' in the cereal box said 'Operation Birthday Surprise' at the top. In big letters. Sam, you have terrible handwriting, but it's not that terrible."
"Then why didn't you say anything?" I asked.
"Because," said Mom, "I wanted to see what would happen. And this is better than any surprise party in the world."

That night, we ate pizza that had been on Uncle Pete, and we ate Bob's retirement cake. Mom said it was the best birthday she has ever had. She has told the story at every family dinner since then. She always ends it the same way: "And that's why you should never hide a secret plan in a cereal box."
Biscuit did not get any cake. He had already had his share.

grammar.name: 一般过去时的被动语态
grammar.zh: was/were + 过去分词，强调动作的承受者
grammar.ex: The gym was covered in pink foam.

grammar.name: 一般现在时的被动语态
grammar.zh: am/is/are + 过去分词
grammar.ex: Volcanoes are made with baking soda and vinegar.

grammar.name: by 引出动作执行者
grammar.zh: 被动句中用 by 说明"被谁"
grammar.ex: the principal was hit by a wave of foam

grammar.name: 情态动词的被动
grammar.zh: can/must/should + be + 过去分词
grammar.ex: Safety glasses must be worn at all times

grammar.name: too … to / enough to
grammar.zh: too + 形容词 + to do 太……而不能；形容词 + enough to do 足够……可以
grammar.ex: The bottle was too small to hold all that foam

items.title: The Science Fair Volcano Was Too Good
items.zh: 科学展的火山太成功了
items.summary: 双胞胎为了赢科学展，把小苏打火山"升级"了十倍。结果体育馆被泡沫淹没、校长被喷了一身，他们却因为另一个原因拿了奖。
paras: Every year, our school has a science fair. It is held in the gym in March, and every student in seventh grade must enter a project. The projects are judged by three teachers and one real scientist from the local university. The winner gets a gold medal, a hundred-dollar gift card, and their photo in the town newspaper.

My twin brother Owen and I have entered the science fair three times. We have never won. In fifth grade, we made a model of the solar system, but the dog ate Jupiter. In sixth grade, we tried to grow plants under different colored lights. All of them died, even the ones under normal light. Last year, we built a robot arm. It was supposed to pick up a cup. Instead, it picked up the judge's glasses and threw them across the room.
This year, Owen had a plan. "We are going to make a volcano," he said.
"A volcano?" I said. "Everybody makes a volcano. Volcanoes are made with baking soda and vinegar. Little kids make them in kindergarten."
"Not like ours," said Owen. He had a strange light in his eyes. "Ours is going to be the biggest, the best, and the most powerful volcano that has ever been made at Riverside Middle School."
I should have said no. I really should have said no.

We worked on the volcano for three weeks. The mountain was built from chicken wire and newspaper in our garage. It was painted brown and gray, and there were little plastic trees on the sides. It was taller than our little sister. Inside the mountain, there was a big plastic bottle. That is where the eruption would happen.

The science part is simple. When baking soda is mixed with vinegar, a chemical reaction happens. The reaction produces a gas called carbon dioxide. The gas makes bubbles, and the bubbles push the liquid up and out of the bottle. That is your eruption. Usually, you use two spoons of baking soda and one cup of vinegar, and you get a nice little fountain of foam.
Owen did not want a nice little fountain. Owen wanted Mount Vesuvius.

"More baking soda means a bigger reaction," he explained. "So we will use ten times more." He also added dish soap, because soap makes the bubbles stronger and longer. And he added red and pink food coloring, because "lava should look like lava."

We tested a small version in the backyard. It worked perfectly. The foam went up about one meter and came down the sides of the mountain like real lava. Our mom took a video. "That's wonderful," she said. "But don't make it any bigger."
We did not test the big version. That was our first mistake.

On the day of the science fair, the gym was full. There were sixty projects on long tables. Parents were walking around. Little kids were running everywhere. The judges were moving from table to table with clipboards. Safety glasses must be worn at all times, said a big sign on the wall. Owen and I put on our goggles. We looked very professional.

Our table was in the middle of the gym, between a project about bean plants and a project about which kind of paper airplane flies the farthest. The bean plant girl looked at our volcano nervously. "Is that safe?" she asked.
"Totally safe," said Owen.

At two o'clock, the judges came to our table. There was Mr. Brooks, our science teacher. There was Ms. Chen, the math teacher. There was Dr. Patel, the scientist from the university. And because it was a special day, the principal, Mrs. Graham, was walking with them. She was wearing a beautiful white suit.
"Tell us about your project," said Dr. Patel.
I explained the chemistry. I talked about baking soda, vinegar, and carbon dioxide. I explained why the soap was added. Dr. Patel nodded. He seemed interested. "Very good," he said. "Can we see it?"
Owen smiled. He picked up a big jug of vinegar. Not a cup. A jug. Two liters. I had not seen that jug before.
"Owen," I whispered. "How much baking soda is in the bottle?"
"Three boxes," he whispered back.
"THREE BOXES?"
But it was too late. Owen poured the vinegar into the mountain.
For one second, nothing happened. Then there was a deep sound, like a giant clearing his throat. The mountain shook. And then the volcano erupted.

It was not a fountain. It was an explosion. A huge column of pink foam shot out of the top of the mountain, straight up, almost to the ceiling. Everyone in the gym turned around. Someone screamed. The foam came down like a pink waterfall, and it did not stop. It kept coming and coming. The bottle was too small to hold all that foam, but the reaction did not care.

The bean plants were the first to go. They were buried in pink foam in three seconds. Then the paper airplanes were swept off the next table. Then the foam spread across the floor in every direction, like a slow pink flood. Kids were laughing and running. Parents were lifting their small children into the air.
And the principal was hit by a wave of foam.

It happened in slow motion. The foam fell from the top of the volcano and landed right on Mrs. Graham. Her beautiful white suit was now pink. Her hair was pink. Her glasses were covered with pink bubbles. She stood completely still.
The gym went silent. Even the volcano seemed to stop and wait.
Owen took off his goggles. "So," he said in a very small voice, "that's the eruption."

The cleanup took two hours. The gym was covered in pink foam. Every mop in the school was used. The janitor, Mr. Lee, said that he had worked at the school for twenty-two years, and he had never seen anything like it. He did not seem angry, though. He seemed impressed. He took a lot of photos.

Owen and I were sent to the principal's office. We sat there for thirty minutes, sure that we would be suspended. When Mrs. Graham finally came in, she had changed into a gym T-shirt. Her hair was still a little pink.
"Do you know," she said, "how much that suit cost?"
We shook our heads. We were too scared to speak.
Then the door opened. It was Dr. Patel, the scientist. He was holding a clipboard, and he was smiling. "Mrs. Graham, may I say something?"

He explained that our volcano was a fantastic example of a chemical reaction that gets out of control. In real science, he said, this is a big problem. Engineers must calculate exactly how much gas will be produced, or tanks and pipes can explode. "These two boys," he said, "just showed sixty students, and their parents, what happens when you don't measure carefully. Nobody in that gym will ever forget it. That is the best science lesson I have seen in years."
Mrs. Graham was quiet for a long time. Then, to our surprise, she laughed. "I suppose," she said, "the suit was a little too white anyway."

We did not win the gold medal. The gold medal was won by the girl with the bean plants, because the judges felt sorry for her, and because her plants survived under the foam, which was actually a very interesting result. But Owen and I were given a special prize. It was a certificate, and it said: "For the Most Memorable Experiment in School History."
Our picture was printed in the town newspaper after all. In the photo, we are standing in front of our volcano, wearing goggles, covered in pink foam. Behind us, you can see Mr. Lee holding a mop.
Next year, Owen wants to study electricity. Mrs. Graham has already said no.

grammar.name: 第一条件句
grammar.zh: If + 一般现在时，主句 will + 动词原形：真实可能发生的条件
grammar.ex: If you give Tyler a drum set, he will play it every day.

grammar.name: unless
grammar.zh: 除非 = if … not
grammar.ex: He won't stop unless you take away the sticks

grammar.name: will 表示预测
grammar.zh: 对将来的判断
grammar.ex: the neighbors will complain

grammar.name: so … that
grammar.zh: 如此……以至于
grammar.ex: The drums were so loud that the pictures on the wall started to shake.

grammar.name: used to
grammar.zh: 过去常常（现在不再）
grammar.ex: Our house used to be quiet.

items.title: If You Give Your Brother a Drum Set
items.zh: 如果你给弟弟买一套鼓
items.summary: 一家人给十二岁的弟弟买了一套鼓，后果像多米诺骨牌一样一个接一个：邻居、狗、奶奶、警察……每一个"如果"都引出下一个麻烦。
paras: Our house used to be quiet. My dad used to read the newspaper on Saturday mornings. My mom used to do yoga in the living room. Our dog, Rocket, used to sleep for fourteen hours a day. I used to do my homework in peace. Those were the good old days. Then my little brother Tyler turned twelve, and my parents made the biggest mistake of their lives.
They bought him a drum set.
I tried to warn them. One week before his birthday, I saw the catalog on the kitchen table. There was a red circle around a picture of a shiny black drum set. I took the catalog to my mom.
"Mom," I said, "I want to explain something to you. It's very important. If you give Tyler a drum set, he will play it every day."
"That's the point," said Mom. "He loves music. His teacher says he has a lot of rhythm."
"If he plays it every day, the house will be loud," I continued.
"He'll practice in the garage," said Dad.
"If he practices in the garage, the neighbors will complain," I said.
"The neighbors are very nice people," said Mom.
I gave up. Nobody listens to the middle child.

On Tyler's birthday, the drum set arrived in five big boxes. Tyler screamed with happiness. It took Dad three hours to put it together. When it was finished, Tyler sat down behind it. He picked up the sticks. He looked at us with a serious face, like a rock star before a big concert.
Then he hit everything at once.
BOOM! CRASH! BANG-BANG-BANG! TSSSSS!

The drums were so loud that the pictures on the wall started to shake. A glass fell off the kitchen shelf. Rocket, who had been asleep on the sofa, jumped two feet in the air and ran under the bed. He did not come out for six hours.
"Wonderful!" said Mom, with her hands over her ears. "Maybe a little quieter, sweetheart?"
Tyler did not play quieter. Tyler did not know the meaning of the word quieter.
So the drums went into the garage. And this is what happened next, exactly as I predicted. I want you to notice that I predicted all of it.

If you put a drum set in the garage, your brother will practice there every day after school. Tyler practiced from four o'clock to six o'clock every afternoon. He played the same rhythm again and again. BOOM-tsss, BOOM-BOOM-tsss. I could hear it in my bedroom, in the kitchen, and in the shower. I could hear it in my dreams.

If your brother practices every day, the neighbors will complain. Mr. Henderson lives next door. He is retired, and he grows prize-winning roses. On the third day, he knocked on our door. He was holding a rose. "This rose," he said, "was beautiful yesterday. Today, all its petals have fallen off. I believe it was the vibration."

If the neighbors complain, your parents will buy earplugs. Mom bought a box of fifty earplugs. She gave a pair to everyone in the family, and she gave a pair to Mr. Henderson. She even tried to put earplugs in Rocket's ears. Rocket did not agree with this plan.

If everyone wears earplugs, nobody will hear anything. This was a bigger problem than we expected. Dad didn't hear the phone ring, and he missed an important call from his boss. Mom didn't hear the oven timer, and she burned the lasagna. I didn't hear my alarm clock, and I was late for school two times. And none of us heard Grandma, who came to visit and rang the doorbell for twenty minutes.

If Grandma waits outside for twenty minutes, she will be angry. Grandma was very angry. She finally walked around the house and came in through the garage. She found Tyler there, playing the drums with his eyes closed. She stood in front of him with her arms crossed. Tyler did not see her for a full minute. When he opened his eyes, he screamed and fell off his chair.
But then something surprising happened. Grandma didn't shout at him. She looked at the drums for a long time. Then she said, "Give me those sticks."

It turns out that Grandma used to play the drums. In 1972, she was in a band. A real band. They were called The Silver Spoons, and they played at weddings and parties all over the state. Nobody in our family knew this. Not even Mom.

Grandma sat down behind the drums. She hit them once, twice, to check the sound. And then she played. She played a long, fast, complicated rhythm. Her hands moved so fast that we could not see the sticks. It was amazing. Tyler's mouth was wide open. Mom's mouth was wide open. Even Rocket came out from under the bed to listen.
When she finished, there was a long silence. Then Tyler said, "Grandma, will you teach me?"
"I'll teach you," said Grandma, "but you have to promise me something. You will learn to play quietly first. A good drummer can play soft. Anyone can play loud."
So now Grandma comes every Tuesday and Thursday. And, of course, things kept happening, one after another.
If Grandma teaches your brother, he will get better. Tyler got much better. He learned real rhythms. He learned to play soft and loud. He learned to listen.

If he gets better, he will start a band. Tyler started a band with three boys from his class. They called themselves The Garage Monkeys. They practiced in our garage on Saturdays. Four twelve-year-olds in one garage. You can imagine the noise.

If he starts a band, someone will call the police. On a Saturday afternoon, a police car stopped in front of our house. A police officer got out. He was young and very serious. He walked to the garage. I thought, this is it. Tyler is going to jail.

The police officer listened for a moment. Then he said, "Is that 'Back in Black'? You're playing it a little too fast." It turned out that he played the guitar. He stayed for forty minutes and gave the band some advice. Then he left, because someone had actually called about a stolen bicycle.
If the band gets good enough, they will want to play a concert. The Garage Monkeys wanted to play a concert. Where? In our backyard, of course. They made posters. They invited the whole street.

If you invite the whole street, Mr. Henderson will come. And he did. He sat in the front row with a cup of tea. We were all very nervous. But when the band started playing, something incredible happened. Mr. Henderson started tapping his foot. Then he started nodding his head. By the third song, he was dancing. He was seventy-eight years old, and he was dancing in our backyard.
After the concert, he came to Tyler and shook his hand. "Young man," he said, "my roses have not recovered. But that was the most fun I have had in twenty years."

So, what is the lesson of this story? I am still not sure. Our house is still loud. My homework is still interrupted every afternoon. Rocket still sleeps under the bed on band days. And I still have to wear earplugs at dinner sometimes.

But I'll tell you one thing that I have learned. If you give your brother a drum set, he will make a lot of noise. Unless your grandma is a secret rock star. Then he will make music. He won't stop unless you take away the sticks, but by then, you won't want him to.

items.title: The Worst Camping Trip Ever
items.summary: 从没露营过的城里一家人，被爸爸拉去"亲近大自然"。帐篷搭反了、熊来偷零食、手机没信号，最后一家人却说这是最好的一次旅行。
paras: My family is not an outdoor family. We are an indoor family. My mom works on a computer all day. My dad works on a computer all day. My sister Chloe and I spend most of our free time looking at our phones. Our idea of nature is the plant in the living room, and it is plastic.
So we were all very surprised when Dad came home one Friday and said, "This summer, we are going camping."
"Camping?" said Mom. "Like, in a tent?"

"In a tent," said Dad. "In the forest. For three days. No Wi-Fi. No TV. Just us and nature." He had a strange, happy look on his face. He had been watching survival videos online for a month. We should have seen this coming.
"Why?" asked Chloe. She is fifteen and she asks "why" about everything.
"To get away from screens," said Dad. "We are going to the mountains to get away from screens. We need to reconnect with nature. And with each other."
"I am connected with you," said Chloe. "We are in the same family group chat."

Dad did not listen. Two weeks later, we were driving into the mountains in a car full of equipment. Dad had bought everything: a big tent, four sleeping bags, flashlights, a camping stove, a first-aid kit, a water filter, and a book called How to Survive in the Wild. He had never opened the book.

The campsite was beautiful. I have to admit that. It was next to a lake, surrounded by tall pine trees. The air smelled clean and fresh. There were birds singing and a small river running into the lake. Mom took a deep breath. "Okay," she said. "This is nice."
Then Chloe looked at her phone. "There's no signal," she said. Her voice was the voice of a person in a horror movie.
"Exactly," said Dad. "Isn't it wonderful?"

The first challenge was the tent. Dad said he didn't need the instructions. "How hard can it be?" he said. It was very hard. It took us two hours. First, we put the tent up upside down. Then we put it up inside out. Then we put it up correctly, but on top of a big rock, right in the middle. Finally, we moved it to a flat place. By then, it was getting dark, and we were all hungry and annoyed.

Dad decided to teach us how to make a fire. He had seen it in a video. He collected sticks and dry leaves. He put them in a little pile. He used a special stick to make sparks. He tried for twenty minutes. No fire. He tried for forty minutes. Still no fire. The sun went down. Mosquitoes came out. Hundreds of them. They loved Dad most of all.
Finally, Mom went to the car and came back with a box of matches and a bottle of lighter fluid. In ten seconds, there was a big, beautiful fire. Dad looked at her. "That's cheating," he said.
"That's dinner," said Mom.

We cooked hot dogs on sticks over the fire. Then we toasted marshmallows. My marshmallow caught fire and became a little black ball. Chloe's fell into the fire. Dad's was perfect, golden brown. He held it up proudly. Then a moth landed on it. We ate them anyway. The marshmallows, not the moths.

After dinner, something happened that I didn't expect. Without our phones, we just sat around the fire and talked. Dad told us stories about his childhood. Mom told us how she and Dad met, which was very embarrassing and very funny. Chloe even laughed, a real laugh, not a phone laugh. Then we looked up.

What a beautiful night it was! I had never seen so many stars. In the city, you can see maybe twenty stars. Here, there were thousands. Millions. The whole sky was covered in them. We could even see the Milky Way, like a long white cloud across the sky. Nobody said anything for a long time. We just looked.
Then we went to bed, and things got bad again.

The tent was too small for four people. My sleeping bag was on a rock. Chloe kicked in her sleep. Dad snored like a motorcycle. And the forest at night is not quiet. There were hundreds of noises. Owls. Insects. Wind in the trees. And something else. Something big, walking around outside the tent.
Crunch. Crunch. Crunch.
"Dad," I whispered. "There's something outside."
"It's probably a raccoon," Dad whispered back. But his voice was not confident.
Crunch. Crunch. Then a loud sniffing sound. Then the sound of something heavy hitting our cooler.
Chloe sat up. "That is not a raccoon," she said.

Very slowly, Dad opened the tent door a little, and he turned on the flashlight. There, next to our cooler, was a bear. A real, black bear. It was not very big, but it was a bear. It had opened the cooler with its paws. It was eating our bacon.
Nobody moved. Nobody breathed.

Then Mom, who has never camped in her life, did something brave. She remembered a sign at the entrance of the campsite. She took two cooking pots and started banging them together. CLANG! CLANG! CLANG! "GO AWAY, BEAR!" she shouted. "GO AWAY!"

The bear looked up. It looked at Mom. It looked very annoyed, like a teenager who has been told to go to bed. Then it picked up the whole package of hot dog buns in its mouth and walked slowly back into the forest.

We stayed awake for the rest of the night. Dad finally opened the survival book with his flashlight. "It says here," he read, "you must never keep food near your tent. All food must be locked in your car." He closed the book. "Good to know."

The next morning, we met the park ranger. She was a friendly woman with a big hat. When we told her about the bear, she laughed. "Oh, that's Gus," she said. "He visits all the new campers. You don't have to be afraid of bears like Gus. He's not dangerous. He just loves bacon. You have to keep your food in the car, though. Gus can open a cooler faster than you can."

On the second day, we went hiking. We got lost for three hours because Dad said he didn't need a map. On the third day, it rained all morning, and the tent leaked. My sleeping bag was wet. Chloe's phone ran out of battery, even though there was no signal. Dad got so many mosquito bites that his arm looked like a map of the stars.
When we finally drove home, we were dirty, tired, and wet. Nobody talked for the first hour. Then Chloe said, "That was the worst trip of my life."
"I'm sorry," said Dad. He looked sad.
"No," said Chloe. "I mean, it was terrible. But it was the best worst trip. Can we go again next year?"
We all stared at her.
"What?" she said. "I want to see Gus again."

It was the most exciting and the most frightening night of my life, and I will never forget it. We are going again next summer. This time, Dad has promised to read the book first. And Mom is bringing more pots.

items.title: Healthy Habits That Actually Work
items.summary: 睡眠、饮食、运动、喝水、屏幕时间和压力——用初中常见的高频词讲清楚每个习惯为什么重要、怎么做。
paras: Everybody wants to be healthy. We all know that we should eat vegetables, sleep more, and exercise regularly. But knowing something and doing it are two very different things. Most people have tried to start a healthy habit at least once. Maybe they decided to go running every morning, or to stop eating junk food. Usually, they lasted about a week. Then life got busy, and the old habits came back.

The good news is that healthy habits do not have to be difficult. You do not need to run a marathon or eat only salad. Small changes, if you do them every day, can make a big difference. In this article, we will look at six healthy habits that actually work, and we will explain why they are important. We will also give you some simple ideas to help you start.
Habit 1: Get enough sleep

Getting enough sleep is the first healthy habit, and maybe the most important one. Sleep is not a waste of time. While you are sleeping, your body is very busy. It repairs your muscles. It makes your immune system stronger, so you can fight colds and flu. And your brain organizes everything you learned during the day. Scientists have found that students who sleep well remember more information and get better grades.

How much sleep do you need? It depends on your age. Children between six and twelve need nine to twelve hours a night. Teenagers need eight to ten hours. Adults need seven to nine hours. But many people do not get enough. In fact, studies show that most teenagers sleep less than eight hours on school nights.

What happens when you do not sleep enough? If you sleep less than seven hours, you will feel tired and hungry the next day. You will find it hard to concentrate in class or at work. You will be in a worse mood, and you might get angry more easily. You will probably eat more junk food too, because a tired brain wants quick energy from sugar.

Here are some tips for better sleep. Go to bed and get up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Keep your bedroom dark, cool, and quiet. Avoid coffee, tea, and energy drinks in the afternoon and evening. And, most importantly, you shouldn't look at your phone for an hour before bed. The bright light from screens tells your brain that it is still daytime, so it is harder to fall asleep. Instead, read a book, take a warm shower, or listen to quiet music.
Habit 2: Eat a balanced diet
The word "diet" does not only mean eating less to lose weight. Your diet is simply all the food you eat. A balanced diet means you eat many different kinds of food in the right amounts.

A healthy plate has four main parts. Half of your plate should be vegetables and fruit. They give you vitamins, minerals, and fiber. Fiber helps your stomach work well. One quarter of your plate should be protein, like chicken, fish, eggs, beans, or tofu. Protein helps you build strong muscles. The last quarter should be whole grains, like brown rice, whole wheat bread, or oats. They give you long-lasting energy. And you need a small amount of healthy fats, from things like nuts, olive oil, and avocados.

The biggest problem in modern diets is sugar. Sugar is hidden in many foods that do not even taste sweet, like bread, ketchup, and pasta sauce. Many teenagers eat too much sugar and too many snacks. A single can of soda has about ten teaspoons of sugar. That is more than the recommended amount for a whole day. When you eat a lot of sugar, your energy goes up very fast, and then it crashes down. You feel tired, hungry, and grumpy.

You do not need to stop eating sweets completely. That is not realistic, and it is not fun. But try to make small changes. Eat fruit instead of candy for a snack. Choose plain yogurt and add your own fruit. Read the labels on food packages. If sugar is one of the first three ingredients, that food has a lot of it.

Another important tip: don't skip breakfast. People who eat breakfast usually have more energy in the morning and eat less junk food later in the day. A good breakfast does not need to be big. Eggs and toast, oatmeal with fruit, or yogurt with nuts are all great choices.
Habit 3: Move your body every day

Exercise is like medicine, but you do not need a doctor to get it. Regular exercise makes your heart and lungs stronger. It builds muscles and bones. It helps you keep a healthy weight. It also improves your mood. When you exercise, your brain releases chemicals called endorphins. Endorphins make you feel happy and relaxed. That is why many people say they feel great after a run or a game of basketball.

Experts say that teenagers should get at least sixty minutes of physical activity every day. Adults need at least thirty minutes on most days. This does not mean you have to go to the gym. Any activity that makes your heart beat faster counts. Walking, biking, dancing, swimming, playing soccer, and even cleaning the house are all exercise.

The secret is to find an activity that you enjoy. If you hate running, do not run. Try something else. Maybe you will love dancing, or rock climbing, or skateboarding. If you enjoy your exercise, you will keep doing it. It also helps to exercise with a friend. You can encourage each other, and it is more fun.

Here are some easy ways to move more every day. Take the stairs instead of the elevator. Walk or bike to school if it is safe. Get off the bus one stop early and walk the rest of the way. Stand up and stretch every hour when you are studying. Play outside with your friends or your dog instead of watching TV.
Habit 4: Drink more water

About sixty percent of your body is water. You lose water all day long when you breathe, sweat, and go to the bathroom. If you do not drink enough, you can become dehydrated. Dehydration can cause headaches, tiredness, and difficulty concentrating. Many people think they are hungry when they are actually thirsty.

How much water do you need? A simple rule is to drink about six to eight glasses a day, and more if it is hot or if you exercise. Water is better than juice or soda, because it has no sugar and no calories. If you do not like plain water, add a slice of lemon, some mint leaves, or a few pieces of fruit.
A great habit is to carry a water bottle with you everywhere. Fill it in the morning, and try to finish it by lunch. Then fill it again. When you see the bottle, you will remember to drink.
Habit 5: Control your screen time

Phones, tablets, computers, and TVs are part of our lives. They are useful for school, work, and staying in touch with friends. But too much screen time can cause problems. It can hurt your eyes and your neck. It can make you sit still for too many hours. It can make it harder to sleep. And spending a lot of time on social media can make some people feel lonely, anxious, or unhappy with their lives.

You do not have to throw away your phone. Instead, try to use it more carefully. Here are some ideas. Check how many hours you spend on your phone each day. Most phones can show you this information. You might be surprised. Turn off notifications for apps that are not important. Keep your phone out of your bedroom at night. Have "no phone" times, for example during meals with your family. And when you have free time, try to do something that is not on a screen at least once a day: read a book, draw, cook, play an instrument, or go outside.
There is also a simple rule for your eyes, called the 20-20-20 rule. Every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds. This gives your eye muscles a short rest.
Habit 6: Manage stress

Everybody feels stressed sometimes. Students feel stressed about tests, homework, and friendships. Adults feel stressed about work, money, and family. A little stress is normal, and it can even help you. It can give you energy to finish a project or to do well in a game. But too much stress for a long time is bad for your health. It can cause headaches, stomachaches, sleep problems, and sadness.

The good news is that there are many ways to manage stress. Exercise is one of the best, as we saw above. Sleeping well also helps a lot. Here are some other strategies. Talk to someone you trust, like a friend, a parent, or a teacher. Just talking about your problem can make you feel better. Write your thoughts in a journal. Try deep breathing: breathe in slowly for four seconds, hold for four seconds, and breathe out for four seconds. Do this five times. Spend time in nature, even if it is just a park. Do something creative, like drawing or playing music. And remember to laugh. Watch a funny video or spend time with funny friends. Laughing really is good medicine.

Another important skill is planning. A lot of stress comes from having too many things to do at the same time. Use a planner or a calendar. Write down your homework, your tests, and your activities. Break big tasks into small steps. For example, if you have a big project, do a little bit every day instead of doing everything the night before. You will feel much calmer.
How to build a new habit
Now you know six healthy habits. But how can you actually make them part of your life? Scientists who study habits have discovered some useful tricks.

First, start small. Do not try to change everything at once. Choose one habit, and make it very easy. For example, if you want to exercise more, start with a ten-minute walk after dinner. If you want to drink more water, start by drinking one glass when you wake up. Small successes give you confidence.

Second, connect the new habit to something you already do. For example: "After I brush my teeth in the morning, I will drink a glass of water." Or: "After I get home from school, I will put on my shoes and walk around the block." Your old habit becomes a reminder for your new habit.

Third, make it easy to do the right thing and hard to do the wrong thing. If you want to eat more fruit, put a bowl of fruit on the kitchen table. If you want to eat fewer chips, do not keep chips in the house. If you want to go running in the morning, put your running shoes next to your bed.
Fourth, track your progress. Use a calendar and draw an X on every day that you do your new habit. After a few days, you will have a chain of Xs. You will not want to break the chain.

Finally, be patient and kind to yourself. Studies show that it takes about two months, on average, for a new behavior to become automatic. You will make mistakes. You will miss some days. That is normal. If you miss a day, do not give up. Just start again the next day. Remember, the goal is not to be perfect. The goal is to be a little bit healthier than yesterday.
Your healthy habits checklist
Here is a simple daily checklist. How many can you do today?

I slept at least eight hours last night. I ate breakfast this morning. I ate at least five portions of fruit and vegetables today. I drank six to eight glasses of water. I moved my body for at least sixty minutes. I put my phone away one hour before bed. I did something to relax or have fun.
Do not worry if you cannot check every box today. Choose one, and start there. Your future self will thank you.

items.title: Making Friends and Getting Along with People
items.summary: 怎么开口认识新朋友、怎么做一个好朋友、怎么处理吵架和道歉、怎么和家人同事相处。都是日常交际最高频的词和句型。
paras: Friends are one of the most important parts of our lives. They make us laugh when we are sad. They help us when we have problems. They share our happy moments and our difficult moments. Scientists have even found that people who have good friends live longer, healthier, and happier lives. But making friends is not always easy, and keeping friends can be even harder. In this article, we will talk about how to make new friends, how to be a good friend, and how to get along with people, even when you do not agree with them.
Why making friends can be hard

Many people find it difficult to make new friends. Maybe you have moved to a new city. Maybe you have started at a new school or a new job. Maybe you are shy, and you feel nervous when you talk to people you do not know. These feelings are completely normal. In fact, most people feel a little nervous when they meet strangers. The difference is that some people have learned how to manage those feelings.

The good news is that making friends is a skill. Like any skill, you can learn it and get better at it with practice. You do not have to be the funniest person in the room, or the most popular. You just have to be friendly, interested in other people, and patient.
Step 1: Be open and friendly

The first step is to show people that you are open to new friendships. One of the easiest ways is to smile. A smile tells people that you are friendly and that it is safe to talk to you. My mom always told me to smile and say hello first. When I was younger, I thought that was silly advice. Now I know she was right. Most people are waiting for someone else to say hello first. If you do it, they will usually be happy and relieved.

Body language is also important. If you stand with your arms crossed and look at your phone, people will think you do not want to talk. Instead, keep your phone in your pocket, look up, and make eye contact. Not too much eye contact, of course. Staring at people is strange. Just look at them naturally when they are talking.
Step 2: Start a conversation

Starting a conversation is the part that scares most people. What should you say? The secret is that you do not need to say anything clever. Simple is best. Here are some easy ways to start a conversation:
Comment on something around you. "This line is so long today!" "Wow, it's really hot in here."
Ask a question. "Do you know what time the class starts?" "Is this seat free?" "How do you know the host?"
Give a compliment. "I like your shoes. Where did you get them?" "That was a great question you asked in class."
Introduce yourself. "Hi, I'm Alex. I'm new here."

After the first sentence, keep the conversation going with questions. People love talking about themselves, so ask about their interests, their weekend, or their opinions. You could ask them about their weekend, their favorite music, or a TV show they are watching. Use open questions, which are questions that need more than a "yes" or "no" answer. For example, instead of "Did you like the movie?", ask "What did you think of the movie?" Then, listen carefully to the answer, and ask another question about what they said.
Step 3: Find things in common

Friendships usually grow from shared interests. If you both love basketball, video games, cooking, or the same band, you will always have something to talk about. That is why one of the best ways to make friends is to join a club, a team, or a class. You will meet people who like the same things as you, and you will see them regularly. Seeing someone again and again is very important. Research shows that people usually become friends after spending many hours together.

So, if you want to make friends, say yes to invitations. Go to the party, even if you feel a little nervous. Join the after-school club. Volunteer in your community. Sign up for a sports team or a music group. Each activity is a new chance to meet people.
Step 4: Be yourself

Some people try to change themselves to make others like them. They pretend to like things they do not like, or they act differently with different groups. This might work for a short time, but it does not create real friendships. Real friends like you for who you are. So be yourself. Talk about the things you really care about. Laugh at the things you really find funny. The right people will like the real you.
What makes a good friend?

Making a new friend is only the beginning. To keep a friendship strong, you need to be a good friend yourself. What does that mean? We asked a group of teenagers, and here are their most common answers.
A good friend is someone who listens to you. When you have a problem, a good friend does not just wait for their turn to talk. They really listen, and they try to understand how you feel.
A good friend is honest. They tell you the truth, even when it is difficult. If you have spinach in your teeth, they tell you. If you are making a bad decision, they tell you, kindly.
A good friend is loyal. They do not talk badly about you behind your back. They keep your secrets. They stand up for you when other people are unkind.

A good friend supports you. They celebrate your successes, and they help you when you fail. They come to your soccer game, your concert, or your birthday party. They send you a message when they know you are having a bad day.
A good friend respects you. They respect your opinions, even when they disagree. They respect your time, your things, and your feelings.

My best friend, Maya, is all of these things. We have been best friends since second grade. That is almost eight years. We have had many arguments, but we have always solved them. She knows me better than anyone else, except maybe my mom.
When friends disagree

Every friendship has problems sometimes. Friends argue. They hurt each other's feelings. They make mistakes. This is normal. Disagreement does not mean the friendship is bad. What matters is how you handle it.
First, try to stay calm. When we are angry, we often say things that we do not really mean. If you feel very angry, take a break. Go for a walk, breathe deeply, and talk later when you feel calmer.

Second, talk about the problem directly. Do not ignore it, and do not complain about your friend to other people. Talk to your friend privately. Use "I" sentences instead of "you" sentences. For example, instead of saying "You always ignore my messages!", say "I felt sad when you didn't answer my messages yesterday." "You" sentences sound like an attack, and the other person will want to defend themselves. "I" sentences explain your feelings, and they make it easier for the other person to listen.

Third, listen to the other person's side. Very often, an argument is really a misunderstanding. Maybe your friend did not answer your messages because their phone was broken, or because they were having a family problem. You will not know until you ask.

Fourth, look for a solution together. Ask, "What can we do so this doesn't happen again?" Maybe you can agree to tell each other when you are busy. Maybe you need to spend more time together. A good solution works for both people.
How to apologize
Sometimes, you will be the one who made a mistake. When that happens, you need to apologize. A good apology is not just saying "sorry." A real apology has three parts.
First, say what you did wrong. "I'm sorry that I told other people your secret."
Second, show that you understand how the other person feels. "I know that made you feel embarrassed and hurt. You trusted me, and I broke your trust."
Third, say what you will do differently. "I won't do that again. From now on, your secrets will stay with me."
Do not add excuses. "I'm sorry, but you were annoying me" is not an apology. Also, do not expect the other person to forgive you immediately. Sometimes people need time. Be patient.

And when someone apologizes to you, try to forgive them. Forgiving does not mean that what they did was okay. It means that you choose to let go of your anger so that the friendship can continue. Holding on to anger for a long time hurts you more than anyone else.
Getting along with everyone

Not everyone in your life will be your friend, and that is fine. But you still need to get along with many different people: classmates, teammates, coworkers, neighbors, and family members. Here are some tips for getting along with people, even people you do not like very much.
Be polite. Say please, thank you, and excuse me. Greet people when you see them. Small manners make a big difference.

Respect differences. People have different backgrounds, beliefs, and opinions. You do not have to agree with everyone, but you should treat everyone with respect. You can say, "I see it differently, but I understand your point."
Do not gossip. Talking about people behind their back can feel fun for a moment, but it destroys trust. If someone gossips to you about other people, they will probably gossip about you too.
Help others. Offer to help a classmate with homework, carry something for a neighbor, or share your snacks. People remember kindness.
Keep your promises. If you say you will do something, do it. If you cannot, tell the person early. Being reliable is one of the most respected qualities a person can have.
Family relationships

We often forget that family members need friendship too. We sometimes treat our family worse than we treat strangers, because we know they will always be there. But family relationships need care, just like friendships.

Spend real time with your family. Eat meals together without phones. Ask your parents about their day. Play a game with your little brother or sister. Tell your grandparents that you love them. Many of these tips also work with family: listen, be honest, apologize when you are wrong, and forgive.
Feeling lonely

Sometimes, even when we try our best, we feel lonely. Maybe you have just moved, or maybe your old friends have changed. Loneliness is a very common feeling. Many people feel lonely, even people who seem popular.

If you feel lonely, remember that it is temporary. Keep trying to meet new people. Reach out to an old friend that you have not talked to for a long time. Send a simple message: "Hey, I was thinking about you. How are you?" Most people are happy to hear from an old friend. And if loneliness makes you feel very sad for a long time, talk to an adult you trust, like a parent, a teacher, or a school counselor.
Taking the next step

Sometimes you meet someone you like, you have a few good conversations, and then nothing happens. You see them in class or at work, you say hello, but you never become real friends. Often, the problem is that nobody takes the next step. So be brave and invite them to do something. Keep it simple and low-pressure: "A few of us are going to get pizza after the game. Do you want to come?" or "I'm going to the library on Saturday to study. Want to join?" If they say no, do not take it personally. People are busy. Try again another time. Each time you do this, you will feel a little more confident.
Final thoughts

Friendship is one of the best things in life, and it is worth the effort. Be brave and say hello first. Be curious about other people. Be honest, loyal, and kind. Apologize when you make mistakes, and forgive others when they make mistakes. And, most of all, be yourself. Somewhere out there, there is someone who is waiting to meet exactly the kind of person you are.

items.title: Technology in Our Everyday Lives
items.summary: 从手机、网络、网购到人工智能，用初中被动语态和现在完成时讲科技怎样改变生活，以及怎样安全上网、识别骗局。
paras: Imagine waking up one morning and finding that all technology has disappeared. There is no phone next to your bed. There is no internet. There is no TV, no computer, and no music app. How would you know the time? How would you talk to your friends? How would you find your way to a new place? For most of us, it is almost impossible to imagine. Our lives have been changed by technology in many ways, and most of these changes have happened in just the last thirty years.

In this article, we will look at how technology is used in our everyday lives: at home, at school, at work, and in our free time. We will also talk about some of the problems that technology has created, and how we can use it safely and wisely.
A short history

Technology has always been part of human life. The wheel, the printing press, the telephone, and the light bulb were all important inventions that changed the world. But the speed of change today is much faster than ever before.

The first personal computers were sold in the 1970s and 1980s. They were big, slow, and very expensive. The internet was used by only a few scientists and universities until the 1990s, when it started to become popular with ordinary people. In those days, connecting to the internet made a strange screeching noise, and you could not use the telephone at the same time.

Mobile phones also became common in the 1990s, but they could only make calls and send short text messages. Then everything changed. The first iPhone was released in 2007. It had a touch screen, a camera, music, and the internet, all in one small device. Other smartphones soon followed. Today, more than six billion people in the world have a smartphone. That is about three out of every four people on Earth.
The smartphone in your pocket

Smartphones allow us to do almost anything from our pocket. A modern smartphone is more powerful than the computers that were used to send astronauts to the moon in 1969. Think about everything we use it for in a single day. We use it as an alarm clock in the morning. We check the weather and the news. We send messages to our family and friends. We listen to music and podcasts on the bus. We take photos and videos. We look up information when we have a question. We pay for things in stores. We use maps to find our way. We watch videos, play games, and read books. We even use it to check our health, like how many steps we have walked or how well we have slept.

All of these jobs used to need different things: a clock, a newspaper, a radio, a camera, a map, a wallet, a library, and a telephone. Now, they have been put into one small device. That is amazing. But it also explains why so many people find it hard to put their phone down.
Communication

The biggest change that technology has brought is in how we communicate. In the past, if you wanted to talk to someone in another country, you had to write a letter. The letter was carried by ship or plane, and it could take weeks to arrive. Phone calls to other countries were very expensive.

Today, billions of messages are sent every day through apps like WhatsApp, WeChat, and others. They arrive in less than a second, and they are free. You can make video calls to anyone in the world and see their face as if they were in the same room. Families who live far apart can have dinner together on a screen. Grandparents can watch their grandchildren grow up from another continent.

Social media has also changed communication. It allows us to share our lives with many people at once. We can follow our friends, our favorite artists, and people with similar interests. However, social media has also been criticized. Some people spend too many hours on it. Some people compare their lives with the perfect photos they see online and feel unhappy. And false information can spread very quickly. We will talk more about this later.
Shopping and money

Shopping has also been changed completely. In the past, you had to go to a store, look at the products, and pay with cash. Today, millions of people shop online. You can buy almost anything with a few clicks: clothes, food, books, furniture, and even cars. The products are delivered to your door, sometimes on the same day.

Online shopping has many advantages. It is convenient. You can compare prices easily. You can read reviews from other customers. You can shop at any time of day or night. But it also has some disadvantages. You cannot touch or try on the products. Sometimes the product looks different from the photo. And many small local stores have closed, because they cannot compete with the giant online companies.

Behind every online order, there is a huge system of technology. Orders are received by computers. Products are found in giant warehouses, often with the help of robots. Packages are scanned, sorted, and loaded onto trucks. Each package is tracked with a barcode, so you can see exactly where it is on a map. The trucks are guided by GPS. This whole system is called logistics, and it is one of the fastest-growing industries in the world.

Money has become digital too. Many people rarely use cash. They pay with credit cards, with their phones, or with their watches. They check their bank accounts on an app and send money to friends instantly.
School and learning

Technology has also changed the way we learn. In many schools, students use laptops or tablets in class. Homework is submitted online. Teachers share videos, quizzes, and presentations. Students can work together on the same document from different homes.

The internet is also the biggest library in history. Almost any question can be answered in seconds. You can learn a new language with an app, watch a video that teaches you how to fix a bike, or take a free course from a famous university. People who could never afford a university education can now learn from the best teachers in the world.

But this also creates a challenge. Because information is so easy to find, some students copy answers instead of thinking for themselves. And not all information online is correct. Learning how to search well, and how to check if information is true, has become one of the most important skills of the twenty-first century.
Artificial intelligence

The newest big change is artificial intelligence, or AI. AI is a type of computer program that can learn from data and do tasks that used to need human intelligence. AI is already used in many places, even if we do not notice it. It recommends videos and songs that we might like. It translates languages. It recognizes faces in photos. It helps doctors find diseases in X-rays. It helps cars park themselves. And now, AI chat programs can answer questions, write texts, and help with homework.

Many people are excited about AI. They believe it will help us solve big problems, like curing diseases and fighting climate change. Other people are worried. They worry that AI will take people's jobs, that it will be used to spread false information, or that it will make mistakes that are hard to notice. Most experts agree that AI is a powerful tool, and that it must be used carefully and responsibly.
Living with devices

All of these devices need power, and anyone who owns a smartphone knows the feeling of panic when the battery is at two percent. Many people now carry a small power bank so they can charge their phone anywhere. Phone batteries also get weaker over time. After two or three years, many phones cannot last a full day. Here is a tip: avoid letting your battery go to zero, and avoid leaving your phone in a hot car. Heat damages batteries.

We also download and upload huge amounts of data every day. When you watch a video, you download it. When you post a photo, you upload it. When your phone updates its apps, it downloads new versions. All of this data travels through cables under the ocean and through towers that are placed all over our cities. A single minute of high-quality video can use more data than all the text messages a person sends in a whole year. And, of course, technology has changed food too: with a delivery app, a hot meal can be brought to your door in thirty minutes.
The problems with technology
Technology has made our lives easier, but it has also created new problems. Here are some of the most important ones.

Screen time. Many people spend more than seven hours a day looking at screens. This can cause eye problems, back pain, and sleep problems. It also means less time for exercise, outdoor activities, and face-to-face conversations.

Addiction. Many apps are designed to keep you using them for as long as possible. They use notifications, likes, and endless scrolling. Some people feel anxious when they do not have their phone. This is sometimes called "nomophobia," which means "no mobile phone phobia."

Privacy. When we use the internet, a lot of information about us is collected: what we search for, what we buy, where we go, and who we talk to. This data is often used by companies to show us advertisements. Sometimes, it is stolen by criminals.

Online scams. Criminals use technology to trick people and steal their money or personal information. Scams are sent by email, text message, phone call, and social media. They are becoming more and more convincing.

False information. Anyone can post anything online. Some information is wrong by accident, and some is wrong on purpose. False stories are often shared more quickly than true stories, because they are surprising or emotional.
How to stay safe online
The good news is that you can protect yourself with some simple habits.

Use strong passwords. A strong password is long and is not easy to guess. Do not use your name, your birthday, or "123456." Use a different password for each important account. A password manager app can help you remember them.

Turn on two-step verification. This means that when you log in, you need your password and also a code that is sent to your phone. Even if someone steals your password, they cannot get into your account.

Think before you click. Be careful with links in emails and messages, especially if they say something urgent, like "Your account has been locked!" or "You have won a prize!" Real companies do not usually ask for your password or bank details by message. If you are not sure, go directly to the official website or call the company.

Protect your personal information. Do not share your address, your phone number, or your school's name publicly online. Check the privacy settings on your social media accounts. Be careful about which apps can see your location.

Check before you share. Before you share a surprising story, check if it comes from a trusted source. Look for the same news on other reliable websites. If it sounds too crazy to be true, it might not be true.
Keep your devices updated. Updates often fix security problems. When your phone asks you to update, do it.
Finding a healthy balance
Technology is not good or bad by itself. It is a tool, like a hammer. A hammer can be used to build a house, or it can hurt your finger. What matters is how we use it.

Here are some ideas for a healthy balance. Have phone-free times, like during meals or the first hour after you wake up. Turn off notifications that you do not need. Use your phone to create, not only to consume: take photos, write, make music, or learn something new. And spend time every day doing things without a screen: talking with your family, reading a paper book, playing a sport, or simply looking out of the window.

Technology has given us incredible powers. We can talk to anyone, learn anything, and buy almost everything from our pocket. The challenge for our generation is to use these powers wisely, so that technology makes our lives better, and not only busier.
