items.title: Jobs and Work: What Do People Do All Day?
items.zh: 工作与职业：大家每天都在做什么？
items.summary: 介绍医疗、教育、物流、建筑、餐饮、科技等常见职业，讲工作日、工资、面试和职场用语。初中阶段最常用的职业和工作类词汇。
paras: Most adults spend about one third of their lives at work. That is more time than they spend with their families, more time than they spend on hobbies, and almost as much time as they spend sleeping. So the question "What do you want to be when you grow up?" is a very important one. In this article, we will look at different kinds of jobs, what people do at work every day, and some useful words and phrases for talking about work.
Why do people work?

The most obvious answer is money. People need money to pay for food, housing, clothes, transportation, and many other things. But money is not the only reason. Work also gives people a sense of purpose. It allows them to use their skills, to learn new things, and to feel that they are useful. Many people make their closest friends at work. And for many people, their job is part of their identity. When you meet someone new, one of the first questions they usually ask is, "So, what do you do?"
Jobs in health care

Health care is one of the biggest areas of work in the world, and it is growing as the population gets older. Doctors are the most famous health care workers. A doctor examines patients, finds out what is wrong with them, and decides on the best treatment. Some doctors are general doctors, who see all kinds of patients. Others are specialists, who focus on one part of the body, like the heart, the skin, or the eyes. Becoming a doctor takes a long time. In the United States, it usually takes about eleven years of study after high school.

A nurse is a person who takes care of patients. Nurses check patients' temperature and blood pressure, give them medicine, clean wounds, and explain things to patients and their families. Many people say that nurses are the heart of a hospital. Nurses often work long shifts. A shift is a period of time when a person works, for example from seven in the morning to seven in the evening. Some nurses work the night shift, from seven in the evening to seven in the morning.
Other health care jobs include dentists, who take care of teeth; pharmacists, who prepare and explain medicine; and paramedics, who drive ambulances and help people in emergencies.
Jobs in education

Teachers help people learn. Kindergarten teachers teach small children to read, count, and get along with others. High school teachers usually teach one or two subjects, like math, history, or English. University professors teach and also do research. Teaching is a job that needs a lot of patience and energy. Teachers do not only work in the classroom. They also plan lessons, grade homework and tests, and meet with parents. Many teachers say that the best part of their job is the moment when a student finally understands something difficult.
Jobs in logistics and transportation
Have you ever wondered how the things in a store get there? Every product you buy, from a banana to a bicycle, has made a long journey. The people who plan and manage this journey work in logistics.

Most goods are carried by trucks for at least part of their journey. But many products also travel by ship, train, or plane. Goods from other countries usually arrive in big metal boxes called shipping containers. A container ship can carry more than twenty thousand containers. At the port, the containers are lifted off the ship by giant cranes and put onto trucks or trains.

Many of these containers then go to a warehouse. A warehouse is a large building where goods are stored before they are sent to stores or customers. Warehouse workers are responsible for receiving, storing, and shipping goods. They unload trucks, check that the products are correct and not damaged, put them on shelves, and prepare orders. Many warehouses use machines like forklifts, and some use robots.

There are also people who work in the yard outside the warehouse. A yard worker checks trucks and trailers when they arrive and leave, and makes sure they are in the right place. One yard worker described her job like this: "My job is to make sure every container goes to the right place. I check the container number, I take photos, and I record everything in the system. If one number is wrong, the container can get lost for days."

Truck drivers carry goods from one place to another. Some drivers do short trips in the same city. Others drive long distances and are away from home for days or weeks. Truck drivers need a special license. They must follow strict rules about how many hours they can drive without resting, because tired drivers are dangerous.

Delivery drivers bring packages to people's homes. Dispatchers work in an office and organize the drivers. They tell drivers where to go, solve problems, and communicate with customers. Logistics is a fast-paced world. Everything has a deadline, and small mistakes can cause big delays.
Jobs in building and repair

Construction workers build houses, roads, bridges, and buildings. It is hard physical work, often outside in hot or cold weather. Electricians install and repair electrical systems. Plumbers install and repair water pipes, toilets, and sinks. Mechanics repair cars and trucks. Carpenters work with wood. These jobs are called skilled trades. They usually need special training, but not always a university degree. Many skilled trades pay very well, because there are not enough trained workers.
Jobs in food and service

Restaurants employ many people. Chefs and cooks prepare food in the kitchen. Servers take orders and bring food to the tables. Dishwashers clean the plates and the kitchen. A restaurant manager is the person who organizes everything: the staff, the schedule, the money, and the customers.

Other service jobs include cashiers, who work in stores and take payments; hairdressers; hotel receptionists; and customer service agents, who help customers on the phone or online. Service jobs need good communication skills and a lot of patience, because customers are not always polite.
Jobs in offices and technology

Many people work in offices. Accountants manage money and taxes for companies or people. Lawyers give legal advice and represent people in court. Marketing workers help companies sell their products. Human resources workers hire new employees and help with problems at work.

Technology jobs are some of the fastest-growing jobs today. Software developers write the code that makes apps and websites work. Data analysts study large amounts of information to find useful patterns. IT support workers fix computer problems for other employees. Many of these jobs can be done from home, which is called remote work.
A typical workday

What does a normal workday look like? Of course, it depends on the job. But many office jobs follow a similar pattern. People arrive at around eight or nine o'clock in the morning. They check their emails and plan their day. There are usually some meetings with their manager or coworkers. A meeting is when a group of people get together to discuss something. In the middle of the day, they have a lunch break, usually thirty minutes to one hour. In the afternoon, they work on projects and try to finish their tasks before the deadline. They usually go home at around five or six o'clock.

Other jobs are very different. Nurses, police officers, firefighters, and factory workers often work in shifts, including nights and weekends. Farmers get up before the sun. Restaurant workers are busiest when other people are relaxing, in the evenings and on weekends.
Bosses and coworkers

At most jobs, you have a boss. Your boss is the person who tells you what to do, checks your work, and helps you when there is a problem. A good boss explains things clearly, listens to employees, and gives praise when people do a good job. A bad boss can make even a great job feel terrible. Many studies have found that people do not leave bad jobs. They leave bad bosses. Your coworkers are also very important. You might spend eight hours a day with them, five days a week. When coworkers help each other, work is faster and more fun. When a delivery driver is sick, for example, a good team finds someone else to deliver the packages so that customers still get them on time.
Money at work

People are paid in different ways. Some people earn a wage, which is money paid for each hour of work. For example, someone might earn twenty dollars an hour. If they work more than forty hours a week, they often get paid more for the extra hours. This is called overtime. Other people earn a salary, which is a fixed amount of money every year, no matter how many hours they work. Salaries are usually paid every two weeks or every month. Some jobs also pay tips, like waiters, or commission, like salespeople.

Many jobs also offer benefits. Benefits are extra things that the company gives, like health insurance, paid vacation days, and money for retirement. When people retire, usually in their sixties, they stop working.
Getting a job

How do people get a job? First, they look for job openings online, in newspapers, or through people they know. Then they apply. To apply for a job, you usually need a resume. A resume is a short document that lists your education, your work experience, and your skills. Many companies also ask for a cover letter, which explains why you want the job and why you are a good choice.
If the company likes your application, they will invite you to an interview. In an interview, the employer asks you questions to learn more about you. Here are some common interview questions:
Tell me about yourself. Why do you want to work here? What are your strengths and weaknesses? Have you ever had a problem at work? How did you solve it? Where do you see yourself in five years?

Some tips for a good interview: arrive a few minutes early, dress neatly, smile, and make eye contact. Learn about the company before the interview. Give examples from your experience. And at the end, ask a question of your own, like "What does a typical day look like in this job?" This shows that you are interested.
Your first job

Many teenagers get their first job while they are still in school. Have you ever had a part-time job? Common first jobs include working in a fast-food restaurant, a supermarket, or a movie theater; babysitting; walking dogs; or cutting grass for neighbors. A first job is not usually exciting, but it teaches important lessons. You learn to be on time, to follow instructions, to work with other people, and to deal with customers. You also learn the value of money. When you have worked hard for four hours to earn sixty dollars, you think more carefully before you spend it.
Important skills for any job
No matter what job you do, some skills are always useful. Employers often call them "soft skills."

Communication: speaking and writing clearly, and listening carefully. Teamwork: working well with other people to reach a common goal. Problem solving: finding solutions when something goes wrong. Being responsible: doing what you promised, on time, without someone checking. Flexibility: being able to change your plans when the situation changes. A positive attitude: staying calm and friendly, even on difficult days.
These skills are not taught in one class at school. You learn them through experience: in sports teams, school projects, volunteering, and part-time jobs.
Choosing a career

Choosing a career is a big decision, and it can feel scary. Here is some advice. Think about what you enjoy and what you are good at. Do you like working with people, with your hands, with numbers, or with ideas? Do you prefer to be inside or outside? Talk to people who do different jobs, and ask them what they like and dislike about their work. Try different things through part-time jobs and volunteering. And remember that you do not have to choose one job for your whole life. Many people change careers two or three times. Your first job is not your last job. It is just the first step.

items.title: Traveling Abroad: From the Airport to the Hotel
items.zh: 出国旅行：从机场到酒店
items.summary: 一次出国旅行的全过程：订票、打包、值机安检、坐飞机、过海关、住酒店、问路、点菜和应对意外。每个环节都有最常用的词和整句。
paras: Traveling to another country is one of the most exciting experiences in life. You see new places, try new food, meet new people, and learn about different cultures. But traveling abroad can also be stressful, especially if you do not speak the local language well. The good news is that English is used at airports and hotels almost everywhere in the world. If you learn the most common words and phrases, you will be able to handle most travel situations with confidence.
In this article, we will follow a family on their trip from the United States to London, England. We will go step by step, from planning the trip to coming home again.
Planning the trip

The Lopez family, Mom, Dad, and their two teenagers, Ana and Marco, have been planning this trip for months. "We are flying to London next Friday," Ana told her friends at school. "We are staying for ten days, and then we are taking the train to Paris for three days." She was very excited.

Planning a trip abroad takes time. First, you need a passport. A passport is an official document that shows who you are and which country you are from. You must have a passport to travel to another country. In many countries, it takes several weeks to get one, so do not wait until the last minute. You should also check if you need a visa. A visa is special permission to enter a country. Some countries require a visa, and some do not. It depends on your nationality and the country you are visiting.

Next, you need to book your flights and your accommodation. Accommodation means the place where you sleep, like a hotel, a hostel, or an apartment. The Lopez family booked their flights online three months early, because flights usually become more expensive closer to the travel date. They also made a reservation at a small hotel in central London.

It is also a good idea to buy travel insurance. Travel insurance pays for problems during your trip, like lost luggage, cancelled flights, or a visit to the hospital. Hopefully you will not need it, but if you do, it can save you a lot of money.
Packing

Packing is an art. Most people pack too much. Here are some tips. Check the weather forecast for your destination. Make a list of everything you need. Roll your clothes instead of folding them, because they take less space and do not get as wrinkled. Choose clothes that you can combine in different ways. And always leave a little space in your suitcase for souvenirs.

Some items should always go in your carry-on bag, which is the small bag that you take with you on the plane. These include your passport, your wallet, your phone and charger, any medicine you need, and a change of clothes in case your suitcase gets lost. Liquids in your carry-on bag must be in small bottles, usually no more than one hundred milliliters each.
At the airport
On the day of the flight, the Lopez family arrived at the airport three hours early. For international flights, it is a good idea to arrive at least two or three hours before departure.

The first step is check-in. Today, most people check in online on the airline's app the day before the flight. You don't have to print your boarding pass. You can show it on your phone. A boarding pass is the document that shows your name, your flight number, your seat, and your gate. At the airport, you go to the airline's counter to drop off your checked luggage. Checked luggage is the big suitcase that travels under the plane. The airline worker weighs your suitcase. If it is too heavy, you will have to pay an extra fee.
"Good morning," said the airline worker. "Where are you flying to today?"
"London," said Dad.
"Can I see your passports, please? Are you checking any bags?"
"Yes, two suitcases."
"Did you pack your bags yourself? Are there any batteries or dangerous items inside?"
"No, nothing like that."
"Great. Here are your luggage tags. Your bags will be sent directly to London. Your flight leaves from Gate 42. Boarding starts at 10:15. Have a nice flight!"

The next step is security. Your bag will be checked at the security gate. You put your carry-on bag, your jacket, your laptop, and sometimes your shoes in plastic trays. They go through an X-ray machine. Then you walk through a metal detector or a body scanner. If the machine beeps, a security officer might check you by hand. It is not fun, but it keeps everyone safe.

After security, there is usually time to relax. Airports have shops, restaurants, and cafes. Marco wanted to buy a snack, but he was worried about missing the plane. He found an airport worker and asked politely, "Excuse me, could you tell me where the gate is? Gate 42?"
"Sure," said the worker. "Go straight down this hallway and turn left. It's about a ten-minute walk. Keep an eye on the screens, in case the gate changes."

Airport screens show all departures and arrivals. They show the flight number, the destination, the time, the gate, and the status. The status might say "On time," "Delayed," "Boarding," "Final call," or "Cancelled." When you see "Final call," you must go to the gate immediately, or the plane will leave without you.
On the plane

The Lopez family boarded the plane and found their seats. Ana had a window seat. Marco had an aisle seat, which is the seat next to the walkway. The flight attendants showed the safety instructions. They explained how to use the seatbelt, where the emergency exits were, and what to do if there was a problem.

The flight to London took about ten hours. During the flight, the passengers were served two meals and some snacks. "Would you like chicken or pasta?" asked the flight attendant. "Chicken, please," said Mom. "And could I have some water, please?"

To make a long flight more comfortable, drink a lot of water, walk around the plane every few hours, and try to sleep if it is night time at your destination. This helps your body adjust to the new time zone. The tired feeling you get after flying across many time zones is called jet lag. Jet lag can make you feel tired, hungry at strange times, and confused for a few days.
Arrival and customs
When the plane landed in London, the passengers went to passport control. A border officer checked their passports and asked them some questions.
"What is the purpose of your visit?"
"Tourism. We're on vacation."
"How long are you staying?"
"Ten days in London, then three days in France."
"Where are you staying?"
"At a hotel near Hyde Park."
"Enjoy your stay."

Then they went to baggage claim, the area where you collect your checked luggage. Bags come out on a moving belt called a carousel. The family waited for twenty minutes. Three suitcases arrived. The fourth one did not. "Oh no," said Dad. "Where's my suitcase?"

They went to the lost baggage desk. "My suitcase hasn't arrived," Dad explained. "It's a big black suitcase with a red ribbon on the handle." The airline worker took his information. "Don't worry," she said. "Most bags are found within twenty-four hours. It will be delivered to your hotel." Luckily, Dad had packed a change of clothes in his carry-on bag. The suitcase arrived at the hotel the next evening.

Finally, they went through customs. Customs is the place where officers check if you are bringing anything into the country that is not allowed, or that you need to pay taxes on, like large amounts of alcohol or cigarettes.
Money

Before leaving the airport, the family needed some local money. The currency in the United Kingdom is the British pound. In France, and in many other European countries, the currency is the euro. You can change money at the airport, but the exchange rate is usually not very good. It is often cheaper to take money from an ATM or to pay with a credit card. Before you travel, tell your bank that you are going abroad, so they do not block your card.
At the hotel
The family took the subway, which Londoners call "the Tube," to their hotel. At the reception desk, Mom said, "Hello, we have a reservation under the name Lopez."

"Welcome!" said the receptionist. "Yes, I have your reservation here. Two rooms for ten nights. We have a standard room on the second floor, or for a small extra charge, a room on the eighth floor with a view of the park."
Mom thought for a second. "I'll take the room with the view," she said.
"Excellent choice. Breakfast is served from seven to ten in the restaurant on the ground floor. Here are your key cards. The Wi-Fi password is on the card. If you need anything, just call reception."
Here are some other useful hotel questions:

What time is check-out? Could I have an extra towel, please? Is there a safe in the room? The air conditioning doesn't work. Could someone fix it? Can you recommend a good restaurant nearby? Could you call a taxi for us?
Getting around the city

In London, the family bought a travel card for the Tube and the buses. Each ticket for a single trip can be expensive, so a weekly card saved them money. They also downloaded a map of the city on their phones, so they could find their way even without the internet. But Mom liked to carry a paper map too. "Phones run out of battery," she said. "Paper maps don't."
Sightseeing

Over the next ten days, the family went sightseeing. Sightseeing means visiting famous and interesting places. They saw Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament. They watched the Changing of the Guard at Buckingham Palace. They rode the London Eye, a giant wheel with amazing views of the city. They visited the British Museum, which is free and has treasures from all over the world. Ana's favorite place was a huge bookstore with five floors. Marco's favorite was a street market where he tried food from ten different countries.

They also took a tour with a guide, a person who shows tourists around and explains the history of the places. The guide was funny and told them many stories about kings, queens, ghosts, and famous writers.
Eating out

Trying local food is one of the best parts of travel. In a restaurant, the server will bring you a menu and ask, "Are you ready to order?" You can say, "Yes, I'd like the fish and chips, please," or "Not yet, could we have a few more minutes?" If you have an allergy, tell the server: "I'm allergic to nuts. Does this dish have any nuts in it?" At the end, ask for the bill: "Could we have the bill, please?" In the United States, people call it "the check."

Tipping customs are different in every country. In the United States, people usually tip fifteen to twenty percent. In the United Kingdom, a service charge is often included in the bill. In Japan, tipping can even be considered rude. Always check the local custom.
Being a good tourist

When you visit another country, remember that you are a guest. Learn a few words in the local language, like "hello," "please," "thank you," and "excuse me." People appreciate the effort, even if your pronunciation is not perfect. Respect local customs. In some places, you have to take off your shoes before entering a home or a temple. In others, you have to cover your shoulders in religious buildings. Be patient and polite, even when things go wrong. And always be aware of your belongings, especially in crowded tourist areas, because pickpockets often target tourists.
Coming home

After two wonderful weeks, the Lopez family flew home. They were tired, their suitcases were full of souvenirs, and their phones were full of photos. Ana had already started planning their next trip. "Next year," she said, "I want to go to Japan." Dad looked at his credit card bill. "Next year," he said, "we're going camping."
